assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reshaped trade theory, empirics and policy evaluation, and extended into macro, growth and productivity work. The Melitz (2003) model and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple export-versus-FDI analysis are widely used workhorse frameworks, and the line of work is well confirmed empirically.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the clear originator of the heterogeneous-firm framework. Helpman is central to the broader new trade theory and to the firm-level extensions. Redding is an important later contributor, especially on quantitative and spatial work, but is more naturally credited elsewhere. A two-person award is cleaner.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across theory, microdata and policy. Trade has not been recognised since 2008, so timing is favourable.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers to pair Helpman with Grossman (B007) instead.
Whether Redding or Bernard/Eaton/Kortum-type contributors should share credit.
Credit for the Melitz-style framework could be spread more widely than the ballot names suggest.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework is the dominant paradigm for monetary policy analysis in central banks and academia. It has had large conceptual, methodological and practical impact through nominal-rigidity models, the Taylor rule and optimal-policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: This is the hardest ballot on attribution, with eight names. Calvo (pricing), Taylor (contracts and rule), Woodford (micro-founded policy analysis) and Gali (Phillips curve and the empirical NK literature) are all plausible. Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets are important for medium-scale DSGE and estimation, but a three-person cap forces hard choices. I pick Taylor, Woodford and Gali, with real doubt about Calvo and Gertler.
assessment.maturity: Decades of use in policymaking. The 2021-23 inflation episode and the HANK literature (B027) have tested and extended the framework without displacing it.
uncertainties: Selecting three of eight is contestable.
Nobel recognition of monetary policy theory already exists (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims, Bernanke).
The framework's performance during the recent inflation surge is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The group built a unified, formal and empirically tested political economics of electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal policy. It is general and spans several fields, with a broad empirical and theoretical research agenda.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the architects of the constitutional and electoral-rules program, which was consolidated in their book and many papers. Besley's work on state capacity and accountability is a close complement. The three-person grouping is coherent.
assessment.maturity: The field has been mature for roughly 25 years, with extensive empirical confirmation. The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson) is related, which may either help or crowd out a political-economy award.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 prize may reduce appetite for another institutions-related award.
Whether Acemoglu-adjacent work already covers much of the ground.
Possible competition from other political economists not listed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data changed how mobility, neighbourhood effects and policy are studied. The work has had major influence on empirical public and labour economics and on policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the leading figure. Hendren and Friedman are close collaborators on the core mobility and neighbourhood papers, but credit is intertwined with a large team. The inclusion of Lawrence Katz is plausible, since his earlier Moving to Opportunity work is foundational. This sorting is a judgment call.
assessment.maturity: Strong, with influential results since 2014 and ongoing replication and extension. Some of it is relatively young and still being validated.
uncertainties: Some findings, such as causal neighbourhood effects and mobility maps, are still being tested.
Credit is spread across a large collaborative team.
Whether the Committee considers the contribution a data-and-measurement advance or a conceptual one.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) credit-cycle model explains how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a core building block of modern macro-finance, and a standard ingredient in work on crises and financial frictions.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the specific mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for financial-accelerator extensions and empirical evidence, but a two-person award is most defensible. Bernanke already shares a related prize.
assessment.maturity: Almost thirty years of confirmation. The Great Recession and later events strongly validated the focus on financing constraints.
uncertainties: Prior recognition of related financial-crisis work (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig 2022) may reduce marginal priority.
Whether Gertler should join Kiyotaki-Moore.
Gertler appears on another ballot (B021), which complicates joint decisions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Historical top-income series from tax data transformed the measurement of inequality and shaped public debate worldwide. The work has methodological and policy influence well beyond academic economics.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the originators of the top-income series, and Zucman's work on offshore wealth and wealth distribution extends them. Atkinson, who is deceased, was central, and credit is shared with the World Inequality Database community.
assessment.maturity: The core series are more than twenty years old. Measurement of the findings is contested, especially for wealth and for post-tax income, and the theory is less developed than the empirical programme.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes about the measurement of top incomes and wealth.
Policy salience may cut both ways in committee judgment.
Zucman's contributions are more recent and are still being evaluated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) and Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) set out a quantitative framework in which misallocation of inputs explains a substantial share of cross-country income gaps. It gave growth and development economics a measurable channel and generated a large literature. It also connects to the questions on productivity and creative destruction I work on.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the most clearly credited for the 2009 framework. Restuccia is closely associated with the broader agenda, and Restuccia-Rogerson is a key co-originator on the ballot's list. Credit is shared and contestable.
assessment.maturity: Strong in citations and use, though there is an ongoing debate about whether measured misallocation reflects true distortions or measurement error and model assumptions.
uncertainties: Measurement error and model-dependence of the misallocation estimates.
Disclosed conflict: Klenow is a long-running co-author of mine, so my view on him should be discounted.
Whether to include Restuccia as the third laureate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic factor models and diffusion-index forecasting are widely used in central banks and macro research for forecasting and structural analysis. The work also contributed to the econometrics of macro time series and weak-instrument problems.
assessment.attribution: Stock and Watson are the central pair for diffusion indexes, forecasting and macro-econometric practice. Reichlin, Diebold, West and Mariano contributed to related lines, notably forecast evaluation and generalized dynamic factor models, but are less central to the core claim.
assessment.maturity: Mature and heavily used, with decades of practical confirmation.
uncertainties: Econometrics was recognised recently (Card, Angrist, Imbens 2021), so the field may be lower priority.
Credit is spread across several distinct sub-literatures.
Impact is more methodological than conceptual.
